alt: A relief carving of an eagle half finished on a CNC router bed, the left half still stepped from roughing, the right half smooth
scene: ON THE MACHINE, wide magazine opening shot from a low three-quarter angle. The carved panel from image 1 is clamped flat on a CNC router's MDF spoilboard, mid-job. THE PANEL IS SPLIT: its LEFT half still shows coarse stair-stepped terraces from a flat roughing cutter, pale bare wood with rough steps and a scatter of chips; its RIGHT half is already smooth from a fine finishing pass, bare pale wood with every feather crisp. A small tapered ball nose cutter in the spindle collet hangs just above the boundary between the two halves. Fresh sawdust on the spoilboard, an aluminium clamp at each corner, the machine's gantry and rails soft in the background. Bright workshop light from the left. No finish or stain yet: this is raw wood mid-cut, but the piece and its design are exactly image 1.

alt: Roughing pass on a relief carving: a flat end mill has cut the design as coarse stepped terraces
scene: CLOSE ON THE MACHINE, IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE ROUGHING PASS ONLY. The panel from image 1 on the spoilboard, but the surface is NOT smooth anywhere: the entire design is cut as coarse horizontal STAIR-STEP TERRACES like a topographic contour map, each step a flat ledge about 2 mm tall with a sharp vertical riser, so the eagle, its wings and the mountains are only recognisable as blocky stepped silhouettes with NO feather detail, NO fine texture, NO smooth curves. A quarter inch flat end mill (straight square-ended cutter, not a ball nose) is in the collet above with chips on it. Raw, pale, completely unfinished wood, no stain, no oil, matte, sawdust everywhere. Bright even workshop light. The terraces are the whole point of this photograph and must be obvious.

alt: Semi-finishing pass with a 1/8 inch tapered ball nose leaving a fine visible scallop pattern across the relief
scene: MACRO on one wing of the panel from image 1, still clamped on the machine, RAW UNFINISHED PALE WOOD with absolutely no stain, no oil, no dark finish anywhere (the finish swatch applies ONLY to the colour of bare cherry, not to any dark tone). The wing is fully formed by a 1/8 inch tapered ball nose pass and its whole surface carries a fine, regular, parallel SCALLOP pattern running diagonally across the feathers, like corduroy or a ploughed field, every ridge about half a millimetre apart, clearly visible in low raking light from the left. The tapered ball nose cutter hangs just above the wing. Fine sawdust in the recesses. Nothing is glossy or dark; this is bare wood mid-job.

alt: Final finishing pass with a 1/16 inch tapered ball nose confined to the eagle's head, sharp beside the scalloped background
scene: MACRO on the eagle's head from image 1, still on the machine. The head and eye have just been cut by a tiny 1/16 inch tapered ball nose at a very fine stepover and are glass-smooth and razor crisp; immediately around it the mountains still carry the faint scallop texture of the earlier coarser pass, so the difference between the two passes is visible in one frame. The tiny cutter hangs above the eye. Raw pale wood, no finish, raking light from the left.

alt: The three cutters that carve a relief, laid beside the finished panel: a flat end mill, a 1/8 inch tapered ball nose and a 1/16 inch tapered ball nose
scene: STILL LIFE on the bench. The panel from image 1, now FINISHED in the house finish, stands propped at a slight angle at the back. In front of it, laid neatly on the maple bench in a row from thick to thin: a quarter inch two-flute flat end mill, a 1/8 inch tapered ball nose cutter, and a 1/16 inch tapered ball nose cutter, all plain unbranded carbide with polished shanks, each about 6 cm long, lying parallel with a little space between. A small brass-coloured collet beside them. Raking window light from the left so the flutes glint. Tight, calm composition; the panel fills about 50% of the frame behind the tools.

alt: A relief panel mid-carve on the machine, half smooth and half still roughed, with the cutter at the boundary
scene: WHERE THE HOURS GO. The design from image 1, EXACTLY as shown and nothing added to it, on the machine bed in raw cherry, no finish: the LEFT half already smooth from the finishing pass, the RIGHT half still in coarse roughing terraces, a tapered ball nose cutter in the collet exactly at the boundary, sawdust piled on the spoilboard. Bright workshop light. ABSOLUTELY NO LETTERS, WORDS, NUMBERS OR CARVED TEXT anywhere on the panel or in the picture; no timer, no clock, no dial.
